title: How we know this
hook: the stories of this century come down through later Sikh chroniclers, Persian records and family memory

segments.voice: Yesterday, the more he cut: Mannu as a sickle, the Sikhs as a crop. Your line was we grow back. What grew back for you? Today, a step back from the stories, to ask where they come from. Day eight hundred seventy-five.

Listen back over the last few weeks on this path and count how often you heard two words: tradition says. Tradition says a brick struck the invader. Tradition says thirty stood. Tradition says the mothers recited the hymns while they ground the grain. Those two words have been doing quiet work all along. They're a signal that a story has come down to us by a particular road. So today, a different kind of lesson. Not what happened. How we know this.
screen: `TWO WORDS: TRADITION SAYS.` → `A STORY COMES DOWN BY A ROAD.` → `NOT WHAT HAPPENED, BUT HOW WE KNOW.`

segments.voice: There are three main roads. The first is the Sikh chroniclers. Long tellings of this century were written down by Sikhs, some well after the events, from what their families and elders had told them. They wrote as insiders, with love and grief, and they kept names and places other records leave out. Tomorrow you'll meet one of them. The second road is the Persian records. The courts and governors of the time kept histories in Persian, and so did some of the writers who traveled with the invading armies. They wrote from the other side, and some wrote with contempt, calling the Sikhs rebels. But they sometimes confirm that a battle happened, or a city fell, even while telling it their own way. The third road is memory. Families who passed stories down. Places like the bunga by the Akal Takht and the gurdwaras of Delhi, which hold a story in stone. And the Ardas, which carries the martyrs into the congregations that say it. Each road has its strengths and its blind spots. Insiders remember what mattered to them. Outsiders record what mattered to theirs. Memory keeps the heart of a story and sometimes rounds off its numbers. So when historians set the roads side by side, they find places where all three agree, and places where they don't. And that's why this path says tradition says. It isn't a sneer, and it isn't a verdict. It's an honest label for how the story reached us. How do we know.
screen: `SIKH CHRONICLERS, WRITING LATER.` · `PERSIAN RECORDS FROM THE OTHER SIDE.` · `MEMORY: FAMILIES, PLACES, THE ARDAS.` · `SETTING THE ROADS SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `HOW DO WE KNOW.`

segments.voice: For this sit, find your own elder. Breathe, and bring to mind someone older who carries a story you only half know: a grandparent, a parent, an old neighbor, a teacher, someone at your gurdwara, church or mosque, or just down the street. What happened that they saw and you didn't? Shape one question you'd like to ask them. Keep it simple. What was it like when. Who was there when. Hold the question, and their face, for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
itihas, history. Sikh chroniclers, Persian records, and memory kept in families, places and the Ardas: the three roads this story of the past has come down to us by. Today's word.
Your line: how do we know. Today, ask an elder the question you shaped, by phone, by text, or in person, and listen to the whole answer. Day eight hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Historians of the Sikh eighteenth century read Sikh chronicles, Persian court histories and oral tradition side by side; in gurdwaras, the same history is carried by the Ardas and by talks called katha.

fork.setup: you're reading about one battle. a Sikh chronicle and a Persian history tell it differently. what do you do?
options: trust the Sikh chronicle and ignore the other.
set them side by side and note where they agree and differ.
trust the Persian one because it's older.
fork.reveal: historians set the roads side by side. where they agree, the ground is firmer. where they differ, they say so.

original.note: Gurmukhi for itihas, history, the Punjabi word for the story of the past.

trapdoor: what you thought: this is just what happened.
what it means: these stories come down by three roads: Sikh chroniclers, Persian records and memory.
what a scholar hears: each source has its own angle, and historians read insider chronicles, hostile court histories and oral tradition against each other.
